newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Sri Lankans, carefree devils of the road.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sri Lankans, carefree devils of the road.

text.p: Drivers stop at the Buddhist shrine and toss in a coin to bring them good luck on their journey. They will need it.
"Jesus Christ will be coming very soon," says the sign on the roadside Catholic Church. Some motorist may well be going to meet his maker sooner than expected.

Overloaded buses career round the corner on the wrong side of the road. Cows wander into the traffic. Truck drivers hurtle out of side roads without looking. Three-wheel scooter taxis weave in and out like angry little gnats.
Welcome to the wonderful world of driving in Sri Lanka where anarchy reigns supreme on the road and the individualist has the right of way.
He who pushes hardest wins in this death-defying sport. A charming, relaxed and courteous people become impatience personified behind the wheel. STICK TO A CHAUFFEUR ON DEADLY ROADS
So it is little wonder that about 100 people a month die on the roads of Sri Lanka, an island with a population of about 18 million, all apparently hell bent on having the road to themselves.
Guidebooks offer solid gold advice to visitors. It is cheaper, safer and wiser to hire a chauffeur to take you round this tropical paradise than to plunge into the kamikaze world of self-drive.

"Driving is very dangerous in Sri Lanka. You have to concentrate all the time," said chauffeur Dissanayke Ratnayaka embarking on a four-day tour of the island with his hand firmly clamped on the horn.

For you have to blast it long and hard to overtake a bus labouring up the twisting passes of the Hill Country or an auto rickshaw wending through villages on the palm-fringed shores of the Indian Ocean. WATCH OUT FOR THE HAZARDS OF THE ROAD
Natural hazards abound from dogs copulating on a mountain road to an old lady in a sari who strides into the traffic without looking left or right.
The bicycle with two children perched on the handlebar suddenly swerves into the road. The driver screeches to a halt when a schoolgirl dashes out without warning.
The moment you step out of the car, touts descend like locusts. Their promises vary widely.
Up in tea plantation country, the boy politely asks: "Do you have spare English coins?"
In downtown Colombo, the wizened pimp in one breath proclaims: "Change money, nice massage, even pretty boy too, no problem." ENJOY THE MYRIAD DELIGHTS OF THE ROADSIDE
It is better to leave the strain of driving to the chauffeur and enjoy the myriad roadside attractions.

Try and catch sight of "toddy tappers" who balance precariously on ropes strung between coconut trees. They are collecting the milky sap of the coconut blossom to make the working man's favourite drink, arrack.
At Weligama, see the stilt fishermen perched on crossbars dangled over the waves on the forked branches of trees. Up rises the chorus of "Money, Money" when your camera is spotted.
You can also work your way through the bounties of nature at the roadside.
In Kalutara, try the delectable mangosteen with its sweet creamy texture and purple skin that stains your clothes indelibly. SAMPLE THE DELIGHTS OF NATURE AT THE ROADSIDE
Slice off the top of a King Coconut for Asia's thirst-quenching answer to the ubiquitous Coca-Cola.
In the fishing town of Chilaw, the bustling fish market provides succulent baked crab.
On mountain roads, the chunky avocadoes are half the price they are in Colombo. Down the coast at Hambantota try curd made from buffalo milk.
And few travellers could resist the sirens of Cadjugama -- colourfully clad women step out and entice you to buy cashew nuts that can be lightly fried in chilli and eaten crunchingly fresh.

After miles of stop-go traffic through the interminable suburbs of Colombo and the crammed coastal villages, the chauffeur sighs with delight as the first clear stretch unfolds invitingly ahead. SPEED GUN TRAPS UNWARY ONCE ROAD CLEAR
Then suddenly from behind a coconut tree out pops a policeman waving his radar speed gun.
Amid the traffic mayhem, the driver had always maintained a zen-like calm but now his composure finally cracks as he pays the 200 rupee (US$3.40) fine.
"Why do they stop me when I finally make it to a stretch of open road?" he asks with a snort of disgust before reaching once more for the horn and accelerator so beloved of the Sri Lankan motorist.
